html:
The siege in 52 BCE in which Julius Caesar trapped Vercingetorix and his army in the Gallic hill town of Alesia, near Dijon in eastern France. It was the last great battle of the Gallic Wars.

Vercingetorix fell back to Alesia with a large army. Instead of storming the hill, Caesar built two rings of ditches, walls, towers and hidden traps around it: an inner ring to hold the Gauls in and an outer ring to keep out the relief army he knew was coming. A similar ring had won the Numantine War eighty years earlier.

Inside, food ran out. The Gauls sent out the town's women and children, and the Romans would not let them through, so they starved between the lines. Then a vast Gallic relief army arrived and attacked the outer ring while Vercingetorix attacked the inner one. Caesar himself led the last counterattack, and the relief army broke.

Vercingetorix surrendered the next day. Organised resistance in Gaul was over. Caesar tells the story in his Gallic War. Digs ordered by Napoleon III in the 1860s found the Roman lines at Alise-Sainte-Reine.
